newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO blame each other for peace crisis.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO blame each other for peace crisis.

text.p: Israelis and Palestinians blamed each other on Monday for what a U.S. official described as a breakdown in the core issues of their 1993 peace accord.
Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said Washington's refusal to pressure Israel had doomed U.S. efforts to revive Middle East peace talks stuck since March.

But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the deadlock stemmed from a Palestinian "crisis of expectations" about their goal of an independent state in lands captured by the Jewish state in 1967.

"We have stopped galloping towards the lines of 1967 that was the basis of Palestinian expectations in negotiations until a year ago," Netanyahu, who took office last year vowing a tougher line in peace talks, told parliament.
"A (Palestinian) state with unlimited self-determination would threaten not only the state of Israel but also other states," Netanyahu said.
The Israeli leader accused Arafat of violating interim peace deals by failing to crack down on "terror" and to cooperate with Israel in fighting militants.

Washington's ambassador to Israel was telling the two sides what they already knew when he said on Sunday Israel's building of Jewish settlements and Palestinian violence had shattered the fragile trust between them.
But Ambassador Martin Indyk's comments appeared to strike a sensitive nerve.
In Gaza, Arafat explained the breakdown by saying: "There is no American pressure to save the peace process."
Palestinians have urged Israel's key ally Washington to press Netanyahu to stop building settlements on occupied lands.
Israel's groundbreaking on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem in March plunged peacemaking into the most protracted crisis since the right-wing Netanyahu was elected a year ago.
The crisis deepened when a Moslem militant blew up a Tel Aviv cafe, killing himself and three Israelis, only days later.
"The core bargain of Oslo has broken down," said Indyk, referring to the landmark 1993 Israel-PLO agreement negotiated in the Norwegian capital.

"Terrorism on the one side and unilateral acts which have created the impression that the final status issues are being pre-empted on the other have combined to break this trust," he told the Israel-U.S. Chamber of Commerce on Sunday.

The Oslo accord, a broad-brush interim agreement that promised security for Israel and self-rule for Palestinians, was aimed at building confidence between the two sides before they tackled thorny "final status" issues.
At times, it did the opposite.

Suicide attacks by Palestinian Islamists opposed to the accord shook the faith of many Israelis in peace while Netanyahu's settlement building convinced Palestinians they would not obtain the state they see as Oslo's natural outcome.
Netanyahu said he was confident peace moves would move ahead if Israel stood its ground.

But Shimon Peres, Oslo architect and opposition Labour party leader since he was ousted by Netanyahu last year, scoffed at the Israeli leader's claims he could salvage the peace process as an "effort to sell a barrel of mustard as a sack of sugar."
"I read in a few newspapers there's a freeze in the peace process. There's no freeze. There's a dynamic deterioration," the Nobel laureate told parliament.
